intro: Matrices (rectangular tables of numbers) can be added and multiplied much like ordinary numbers, but with some surprising differences. This branch learns that arithmetic and how to undo a matrix with its inverse.

VII.3.01.what: The basic vocabulary of matrices: rectangular tables of numbers arranged in rows and columns.

levels.a: Identifies the rows (across) and columns (down) of a matrix.
levels.b: Locates an entry by its row number and column number.
levels.c: States a matrix's size as rows by columns.
levels.d: Recognizes special shapes such as square, diagonal and triangular matrices.

VII.3.02.what: Adding matrices and multiplying them by a single number, done one entry at a time.

levels.a: Knows only matrices of the same size can be added.
levels.b: Adds two matrices by adding matching entries.
levels.c: Multiplies every entry of a matrix by the same number.
levels.d: Uses the familiar rules, such as order not mattering when adding.

VII.3.03.what: Multiplying a matrix by a vector produces a new vector. It is the basic way a matrix acts on things.

levels.a: Multiplies by pairing each row with the vector and adding products.
levels.b: Sees the result as a mix of the matrix's columns.
levels.c: Checks the sizes match before multiplying.
levels.d: Uses the fact that this multiplication respects adding and scaling.

VII.3.04.what: Multiplying two matrices together, which combines two actions into one.

levels.a: Checks which sizes can be multiplied and the size of the result.
levels.b: Computes each entry of the product from a row and a column.
levels.c: Computes the product one column at a time.
levels.d: Sees the product as doing one action and then the other.

VII.3.05.what: The rules of matrix arithmetic, including the surprise that order matters: A times B is often different from B times A.

levels.a: Finds examples where swapping the order changes the product.
levels.b: Uses the rules that do still hold, such as regrouping and expanding brackets.
levels.c: Sees that you cannot simply cancel a matrix from both sides.
levels.d: Computes powers of a matrix by repeated multiplication.

VII.3.06.what: The identity matrix acts like the number 1 and the zero matrix like 0. Some odd matrices become zero when multiplied by themselves.

levels.a: Recognizes the identity matrix: 1s down the diagonal, 0s elsewhere.
levels.b: Recognizes the zero matrix and its role.
levels.c: Shows multiplying by the identity leaves any matrix unchanged.
levels.d: Finds nonzero matrices whose powers eventually become zero.

VII.3.07.what: The transpose flips a matrix over its diagonal, so rows become columns.

levels.a: Writes the transpose by turning rows into columns.
levels.b: Uses the rule that transposing a product reverses the order.
levels.c: Recognizes symmetric matrices, which equal their own transpose.
levels.d: Writes a dot product as a row times a column.

VII.3.08.what: The inverse of a matrix undoes it, like dividing undoes multiplying. For 2-by-2 matrices there is a short formula.

levels.a: Uses the formula to find the inverse of a 2-by-2 matrix.
levels.b: Recognizes when the formula breaks down and no inverse exists.
levels.c: Solves a system of equations by multiplying by the inverse.
levels.d: Checks an inverse by multiplying back to get the identity.

VII.3.09.what: Finding the inverse of a larger matrix using the same row operations used to solve equations.

levels.a: Places the identity matrix beside the matrix to start.
levels.c: Reads the inverse from the right-hand half.
levels.d: Recognizes during the process when no inverse exists.

VII.3.10.what: A single big theorem listing many facts about a square matrix that are all true together or all false together, such as having an inverse.

levels.a: Lists the equivalent facts, such as having an inverse and a pivot in every column.
levels.b: Uses one known fact to conclude the others.
levels.c: Knows the theorem applies only to square matrices.
levels.d: Uses quick checks to decide whether a matrix is invertible.

VII.3.11.what: Each row operation can be carried out by multiplying by a simple matrix, which explains why row reduction works.

levels.a: Writes a single row operation as a matrix.
levels.b: Finds the matrix that undoes each such operation.
levels.c: Writes an inverse as a product of these simple matrices.
levels.d: Explains why row reduction finds inverses and solutions.

VII.3.12.what: LU factorization splits a matrix into two triangular pieces, a shortcut computers use to solve many systems quickly.

levels.a: Recognizes a matrix written as lower-triangular times upper-triangular.
levels.b: Builds the two pieces from the steps of elimination.
levels.c: Solves a system in two easy triangular stages.
levels.d: Explains why this saves work when solving many similar systems.
